title: Business Law

pattern.summary: 9 or 10 questions, attempt any 5, each carries 20 marks. All theory; the last question is short notes with a choice. Quote the section of the Act and give a short illustration (A contracts with B …) in every answer.

choosing: Sale of Goods (conditions and warranties, caveat emptor, delivery, unpaid seller) and Negotiable Instruments appear in every paper.
Contract basics (essentials of a valid contract), guarantee (rights of surety) and bailment repeat very often — easy full-length answers.
Law answers score best as: definition with section number → essentials/rules as headed points → a short illustration (A, B) → exceptions → conclusion.

topics.name: Sale of Goods Act
topics.summary: Contract of sale, goods, conditions and warranties, caveat emptor, transfer of ownership, delivery, sale by non-owners, unpaid seller.
points: Contract of sale (Sec 4): seller transfers or agrees to transfer property in goods to the buyer for a price. Sale (property passes now) vs agreement to sell (passes later/on conditions); risk follows ownership.
Goods: every kind of movable property except actionable claims and money. Types: existing (specific, ascertained, unascertained), future, contingent.
Condition: stipulation essential to the main purpose — breach allows rejection. Warranty: collateral — breach allows only damages.
Implied conditions: title, sale by description, sample, fitness for purpose, merchantable quality, wholesomeness. Implied warranties: quiet possession, freedom from encumbrance.
Caveat emptor (let the buyer beware); exceptions: fitness for purpose relied on seller's skill, merchantable quality, sale by sample/description, usage of trade, fraud.
Transfer of ownership: specific goods in deliverable state — at contract; unascertained goods — on appropriation; sale or return — on approval.
Delivery: actual, symbolic or constructive; rules on place, time, expenses, short or excess delivery, instalments.
Sale by non-owners: generally no better title (nemo dat), except mercantile agent, joint owner, voidable contract, seller/buyer in possession, estoppel.

Unpaid seller: not fully paid. Rights against goods: lien, stoppage in transit, resale. Against buyer: suit for price, damages. Lien is lost on delivery; stoppage in transit applies while goods are with a carrier and the buyer is insolvent.
Sale vs hire-purchase: in a sale ownership passes at once or on the agreed date; in hire-purchase the hirer becomes owner only after the last instalment and may return the goods before that.

Destruction of goods: if specific goods perish without the seller's knowledge before the contract, the agreement is void (Sec 7); if they perish before risk passes, without fault of either party, an agreement to sell becomes void (Sec 8).
topics.frame: Definition with section → rules/exceptions as headed points with an illustration → conclusion.
mistakes: Mixing up lien (goods still with seller) and stoppage in transit (goods with carrier).

topics.name: Negotiable Instruments
topics.summary: Promissory note, bill of exchange, cheque, endorsement, crossing, holder in due course, presentment, lost/stolen/forged instruments.
points: Negotiable instrument: promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque payable to order or bearer (Sec 13). Features: freely transferable, holder in due course gets good title, presumptions of consideration and date.

Promissory note (Sec 4): unconditional written promise by the maker to pay. Bill of exchange (Sec 5): unconditional written order to pay; three parties — drawer, drawee, payee. Cheque (Sec 6): bill drawn on a banker, payable on demand.
Holder vs holder in due course (Sec 9): HDC took it for value, before maturity, in good faith — gets a better title than the transferor.
Endorsement: signing to transfer. Kinds: blank, special/full, restrictive, partial, conditional, sans recourse, facultative.
Crossing: general (two parallel lines, pay through a bank), special (bank named), account payee, not negotiable.
Presentment for acceptance (bills payable after sight) and for payment: at proper place, time, by the holder.
Negotiation (by delivery/endorsement, HDC gets good title, no notice) vs assignment (by written document, assignee gets transferor's title, notice needed).
Lost or stolen instrument: the finder gets no title, but an HDC from the finder does; forged instrument: nobody gets title through a forged endorsement.
A bank may refuse a cheque: insufficient funds, stale (over 3 months), post-dated, mutilated, signature mismatch, stop-payment order, account closed, insolvency or death of the customer.
Inchoate instrument: signed stamped paper left blank — holder may complete it. Hundi: indigenous negotiable instrument.
Maturity: three days of grace are added to notes and bills not payable on demand; if the due date is a public holiday, the instrument is due on the next business day (Secs 22–25).

Dishonour by non-acceptance: the drawee does not accept within 48 hours, gives a qualified acceptance, cannot be found, is incompetent, fictitious, dead or insolvent. Dishonour by non-payment: the party liable fails to pay when it is duly presented.

Discharge of a party (the instrument remains negotiable) vs discharge of the instrument (all rights end). Modes include cancellation, release, payment in due course and material alteration without consent.
topics.frame: Definition with section → essentials as headed points → comparison table (PN vs bill vs cheque) → conclusion.

units.title: Promissory Note, Bills of Exchange and Cheque

topics.name: Discharge, Breach, Remedies & Quasi Contracts
topics.summary: Modes of discharge, supervening impossibility, breach and remedies (damages, specific performance, injunction, quantum meruit), quasi and contingent contracts.
points: Discharge by: performance, mutual agreement (novation, rescission, alteration, remission, waiver), impossibility, lapse of time, operation of law (death, insolvency, merger), breach.

Supervening impossibility (Sec 56): contract becomes void if performance becomes impossible later — destruction of subject matter, death or incapacity, change of law, war. Not covered: difficulty, commercial hardship, strikes, failure of third party.
Breach: actual or anticipatory.

Remedies: rescission, damages (ordinary, special, exemplary, nominal — Hadley v Baxendale remoteness rule), specific performance (where money is not adequate, e.g. unique property), injunction, quantum meruit (payment for work done).
Quasi contracts (Secs 68–72): necessaries supplied to an incapable person, payment by an interested person, benefit of a non-gratuitous act, finder of goods, money paid by mistake or coercion.
Contingent contract (Sec 31): performance depends on an uncertain future event; enforceable only when the event happens.

Performance: the promisor, their agent or legal representatives must perform; performance can be demanded by the promisee (or their representatives). Where time is of the essence, delay lets the other party avoid the contract.
topics.frame: Meaning → modes/remedies as headed points with a case or illustration → conclusion.

units.title: Remedies for Breach and Quasi Contracts

topics.name: Offer & Acceptance
topics.summary: Offer and its legal rules, types of offer, invitation to offer, acceptance, communication, revocation and lapse.
points: Offer/proposal (Sec 2(a)): willingness to do or abstain, to obtain the other's assent.
Rules: must intend legal relations, terms certain, communicated, not a mere statement of intention, not an invitation to offer, may be conditional, cannot make silence acceptance.

Types: express, implied, general (to the public — Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co.), specific, cross offers (identical offers crossing — no contract until one accepts), standing/continuing offer, counter-offer (rejects the original).
Invitation to offer: price lists, goods on display, advertisements, tenders — not offers.
Acceptance (Sec 2(b)): absolute and unqualified, communicated in the prescribed or usual manner, by the offeree, while the offer is open.
Communication: offer complete when it reaches the offeree; acceptance complete against the proposer when posted, against the acceptor when it reaches the proposer.
Revocation: offer can be revoked before acceptance is complete against the proposer; acceptance before it reaches the proposer.
Lapse: after the time fixed or reasonable time, death or insanity of offeror, rejection or counter-offer, failure of a condition.
topics.frame: Definition with section → rules as headed points each with an illustration → conclusion.

topics.name: Nature & Essentials of a Contract
topics.summary: Contract and agreement, essentials of a valid contract, types of contracts, void/voidable/illegal.
points: Contract = agreement enforceable by law (Sec 2(h)); agreement = offer + acceptance. 'All contracts are agreements but all agreements are not contracts.'
'Law of contract is not the whole law of agreements nor the whole law of obligations' (Salmond): it covers only agreements that create legal obligations, and only obligations arising from agreements.

Essentials (Sec 10): offer and acceptance, intention to create legal relations, free consent, competent parties, lawful consideration, lawful object, not expressly declared void, certainty, possibility of performance, legal formalities.
By creation: express, implied, quasi. By execution: executed, executory. By enforceability: valid, void, voidable, illegal, unenforceable.

Void agreement: not enforceable from the start. Voidable contract: enforceable at the option of one party (e.g. consent by coercion). Illegal agreement: forbidden by law — void, and collateral agreements are also void.
topics.frame: Definition with section → essentials as headed points with illustrations → conclusion.

topics.name: Partnership & LLP
topics.summary: Partnership and its tests, kinds of partners, registration, rights of partners, dissolution, LLP.
points: Partnership (Sec 4, 1932 Act): relation between persons who agree to share profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all. Mutual agency is the true test; profit sharing alone is not conclusive.
Kinds of partners: active, sleeping, nominal, partner by estoppel/holding out, minor admitted to benefits, secret, sub-partner, incoming and outgoing partners.

Registration (Sec 58–59): application to the Registrar with firm name, place, partners' names and addresses, date of joining, duration. Non-registration: firm cannot sue third parties or partners; partners cannot sue the firm — third parties can still sue the firm.

Implied authority of a partner: acts in the usual course of business (buy and sell goods, receive payments, engage employees) — not to submit to arbitration, compromise claims, open a bank account in own name.
Dissolution of partnership (change in relations; firm may continue) vs dissolution of firm (business ends). Modes: by agreement, compulsory, on contingencies, by notice, by court.

LLP (LLP Act 2008): body corporate with separate legal entity, perpetual succession, limited liability, minimum 2 partners, 2 designated partners. Differs from a partnership (liability, entity) and from a company (flexible internal management, no share capital).
Partnership differs from co-ownership (no business or mutual agency needed) and from a joint Hindu family business (arises by birth, the karta manages, no agreement).

On dissolution, accounts are settled in order: losses (including capital deficiencies) are paid first out of profits, then capital, then partners personally; assets go to third-party debts, then partners' advances, then capital, and any surplus is shared in the profit ratio (Sec 48).
topics.frame: Definition with section → essentials as headed points → comparison table → conclusion.

units.title: Rights, Duties and Liabilities of Partners

topics.name: Free Consent (Coercion, Undue Influence, Fraud)
topics.summary: Consent and free consent, coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, mistake.
points: Consent (Sec 13): agreeing on the same thing in the same sense. Free consent (Sec 14): not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or mistake.
Coercion (Sec 15): committing or threatening an act forbidden by the IPC, or unlawful detention of property, to make a person agree.
Undue influence (Sec 16): a person in a position to dominate another's will uses it to get an unfair advantage (doctor–patient, guardian–ward). Pardanashin women get special protection.
Coercion vs undue influence: physical threat vs mental pressure; any person vs a party in a relationship; criminal act vs not criminal.

Fraud (Sec 17): false statement knowingly made, active concealment, a promise made without intention to perform — with intent to deceive and the other party actually deceived and suffering loss. Mere silence is not fraud unless there is a duty to speak or silence is itself deceptive.
Misrepresentation (Sec 18): false statement made innocently. Effect: contract voidable at the option of the aggrieved party; fraud also allows damages.

Mistake: of law or of fact. Mistake of Indian law is no excuse — the contract stays valid (Sec 21); mistake of foreign law is treated as a mistake of fact. A bilateral mistake of an essential fact makes the agreement void (Sec 20); a unilateral mistake generally does not (Sec 22).
topics.frame: Definition with section → elements as headed points → illustration → effect on the contract.

topics.name: Agency
topics.summary: Agent and principal, creation of agency (incl. ratification), irrevocable agency, rights and duties of agent, sub-agent, termination.
points: Agent (Sec 182): person employed to do any act for another or represent another; principal: the person represented. Any person may be an agent — even a minor (the principal is liable, not the minor).
Creation: express, implied (e.g. a wife living with her husband can pledge his credit for necessaries; not if living separately without allowance), by necessity, by estoppel, by ratification.

Ratification: principal later adopts an act done without authority. Requisites: agent acted for the principal, principal existed and was competent then and now, full knowledge, whole act ratified, within reasonable time, act must be lawful.
Irrevocable agency: agency coupled with interest; or after the agent has partly exercised authority incurring liability.

Duties of agent: follow instructions/custom, reasonable skill, render accounts, not deal on own account, pay sums received, not delegate. Rights: remuneration, retainer, lien, indemnity, compensation for injury.
Sub-agent: appointed by the agent — agent is responsible; substituted agent: named by the agent on the principal's authority — directly responsible to the principal.
Classification: general, special, universal; mercantile agents (factor, broker, auctioneer, del credere agent).
Termination: by act of parties (revocation, renunciation), by operation of law (completion, expiry, death, insanity, insolvency, destruction of subject matter).
topics.frame: Definition with section → headed points with illustrations → conclusion.

topics.name: Bailment, Pledge & Finder of Goods
topics.summary: Bailment and its kinds, rights and duties of bailee, lien, finder of goods, pledge and pledge by non-owners.
points: Bailment (Sec 148): delivery of goods for a purpose on the contract that they will be returned or disposed of as directed. Essentials: delivery of goods (movable), for a purpose, return of the same goods.
Kinds: gratuitous or non-gratuitous; for the benefit of bailor, bailee or both.
Duties of bailee: reasonable care, not use goods for unauthorised purposes, not mix goods, return goods and any increase. Rights: compensation, reimbursement of expenses, lien, sue third parties.
Lien: right to retain goods until dues are paid. Particular lien (goods on which labour was spent) vs general lien (bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys, policy brokers for any balance).
Finder of goods: has the rights and duties of a bailee; may retain goods until compensated; may sell if goods are perishable or charges reach two-thirds of their value.

Pledge (Sec 172): bailment of goods as security for a debt. Pledge by non-owners is valid in some cases: mercantile agent, person with a voidable title, seller or buyer in possession, co-owner in possession.
topics.frame: Definition with section → essentials → rights and duties in two lists → conclusion.

topics.name: Indemnity & Guarantee
topics.summary: Contract of indemnity vs guarantee, surety's rights against the debtor, creditor and co-sureties, continuing guarantee, discharge of surety.
points: Indemnity (Sec 124): one party promises to save the other from loss — two parties, primary liability.

Guarantee (Sec 126): to perform the promise or discharge the liability of a third person on default — three parties (creditor, principal debtor, surety); surety's liability is secondary and co-extensive.
Rights of surety: against principal debtor — subrogation, indemnity; against creditor — securities held by the creditor; against co-sureties — contribution in equal shares.
Continuing guarantee (Sec 129): extends to a series of transactions; revoked by notice (future transactions) or by the surety's death.

Surety discharged by: variance in terms without consent, release or discharge of the principal debtor, creditor compounding or giving time, creditor's act impairing surety's remedy, loss of security, revocation.
topics.frame: Definitions → comparison table (indemnity vs guarantee) → rights under three headings → conclusion.

topics.name: Consideration & Privity
topics.summary: Consideration and its legal rules, 'no consideration no contract' and its exceptions, stranger to a contract.
points: Consideration (Sec 2(d)): at the desire of the promisor, the promisee or any other person has done or abstained, or does or promises to do or abstain.

Rules: at the desire of the promisor; may move from the promisee or any other person; past, present or future; need not be adequate but must have some value in law; must be real and lawful; not an existing legal duty.

No consideration, no contract (Sec 25) — exceptions: written registered agreement made out of natural love and affection, compensation for past voluntary service, promise to pay a time-barred debt (written and signed), completed gifts, agency.
Privity: a stranger to a contract cannot sue (Tweddle v Atkinson) — exceptions: trust or charge, marriage settlements, acknowledgement or estoppel, assignment, covenants running with land, agency.
topics.frame: Definition with section → rules as headed points with illustrations → exceptions → conclusion.

topics.name: Capacity to Contract (Minor, Unsound Mind)
topics.summary: Competent parties, minor's agreements, necessaries, persons of unsound mind, pardanashin women.
points: Competent (Sec 11): of the age of majority, of sound mind, not disqualified by law.
Minor's agreement is void ab initio (Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose); no ratification on attaining majority; no estoppel; minor can be a promisee or beneficiary and can be an agent.
Necessaries (Sec 68): supplier of necessaries suited to the minor's condition in life can recover from the minor's property, not personally.
Unsound mind (Sec 12): cannot understand the contract and judge its effect on his interests; a person usually of unsound mind can contract during lucid intervals.
Disqualified: alien enemies, foreign sovereigns, convicts, insolvents.
Pardanashin woman: undue influence is presumed; the other party must prove she understood the contract.
topics.frame: Definition with section → rules as headed points with a case name → conclusion.

topics.name: Void Agreements & Public Policy
topics.summary: Agreements in restraint of trade, opposed to public policy, unlawful object or consideration, wagering agreements.
points: Restraint of trade (Sec 27) is void. Exceptions: seller of goodwill agreeing not to compete within local limits, partners' agreements, trade combinations regulating business, service agreements during employment.

Opposed to public policy: trading with enemy, stifling prosecution, interference with justice, marriage brokerage, restraint of marriage (Sec 26), restraint of legal proceedings (Sec 28), sale of public offices.
Unlawful object or consideration (Sec 23): forbidden by law, defeats law, fraudulent, injurious to person or property, immoral, opposed to public policy.

Wagering agreement (Sec 30): promise to pay on an uncertain event with no other interest — void; collateral transactions are valid (except in Maharashtra and Gujarat). Not wagers: insurance, lotteries under licence, prize competitions of skill.
topics.frame: Rule with section → exceptions with illustrations → conclusion.
